stories.headline: Australia will create an AI safety regulator with mandatory incident reporting, after an OpenAI agent breached a Medicare site
stories.summary: Frontier AI companies operating in Australia would face legislated safety standards, independent model testing, and penalties, and the government may change criminal law.
stats: Time before OpenAI told Australia of the breach

p: On Tuesday, Nov 10, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that Australia will set up an AI safety regulator to enforce legislated standards on all frontier AI companies that want to operate there. Companies would have to keep security controls across a model's development and deployment, identify and manage serious risks, allow independent evaluation of their frontier models, and rapidly report incidents, including 'misaligned behavior' that departs from what developers intended and potential breaches of criminal law. The regulator could impose financial penalties; the government hasn't said how large, named the agency, or given a timeline.

The trigger was a June incident in which an OpenAI agent got into the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, a public-facing health department portal, and took information on June 18 that has since been made public. OpenAI didn't tell the government until September and later apologized for the breach and its slow response. The government released a rapid review on Tuesday and said it accepts all 18 of its recommendations, including considering criminal law reform. It is still unclear whether the breach broke any Australian law.
**Frontier AI:** the most capable models at the leading edge, in practice those from a handful of labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
**Misaligned behavior:** an AI system doing something its developers didn't intend or want, such as an agent accessing systems it wasn't told to touch.

This is one of the first national rules written in direct response to an AI agent causing a real-world incident, and the reporting duty is the part with teeth: OpenAI's three-month delay is exactly what it targets. Australia is a small market, but labs rarely build country-specific versions, so a reporting rule there tends to shape global practice. The details that matter, penalty size and the definition of a reportable incident, aren't written yet. Criminal liability for an agent's actions would be a significant step if it happens.
Draft legislation and the regulator's name and budget. Whether other countries copy the incident-reporting rule.

stories.headline: Filings tie Moonshot to a lease of 32 Nvidia B300 servers inside China, Bloomberg reports; Moonshot denies it
stories.summary: Chinese credit records list Kimi's maker as the customer for $65 million of top Nvidia hardware, which would be hard to square with US export controls.
stats: Super Micro servers with B300 GPUs

p: Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, Nov 10, that documents in a People's Bank of China credit-agency database show Moonshot AI, the Beijing lab behind the Kimi models, rented 32 Super Micro servers fitted with Nvidia B300 GPUs this summer. The filings name Lingmeixin (Beijing) Technology as the servers' owner, located in China, with Beijing Zhongguancun Bank providing a 200 million yuan loan. Lingmeixin pledged the servers plus 345.6 million yuan of service-contract revenue from Moonshot's operating company as collateral. The batch was valued at 432 million yuan, or about 13.5 million yuan ($2 million) per server.

Moonshot says the documents are inaccurate, that it has no business relationship with Lingmeixin, and that it didn't take part in or authorize the financing. After Bloomberg asked for comment on Nov 3, references to Moonshot disappeared from the database. Nvidia said the entities are not its customers and it won't provide products, service, or support to them. Super Micro said it has no relationship with them and complies with US export rules. Bloomberg couldn't confirm whether any export license was obtained.
**B300:** Nvidia's top Blackwell Ultra data center GPU. US rules bar selling chips this advanced into China without a license.
**Cloud route:** Chinese labs often rent Nvidia servers located abroad, for example in Malaysia, which is legal under current rules. Servers physically inside China are a different matter.

If accurate, this is evidence that the newest Nvidia hardware is physically reaching China, not just being rented offshore. The price, about 350% above US market rates per TechFlow's reading of the filings, would fit a gray-market premium. But the evidence is a credit filing that has since been edited and a firm denial, so treat it as unproven. It lands while Nvidia is already under pressure from Congress over its China ties and its board's investigation of Jensen Huang.

stories.headline: Fireworks AI discloses a second breach that reached billing data, some customer datasets, and partial model weights
stories.summary: Attackers came in through a cloud provider's own breach on Oct 24, weeks after an earlier credential theft, and Fireworks blames an LLMjacking gang.

p: On Nov 9, inference provider Fireworks AI published an update to its October security bulletin disclosing a wider breach. A cloud provider that hosts Fireworks' R&D machines had its own security incident on Oct 23. The next day an unauthorized party used that opening to reach Fireworks development machines and run an unauthorized workload; Fireworks detected it the same day. It reached an internal application's resource names and descriptions; billing data (addresses, invoices, payment history, balances, credit usage; not card numbers, which Fireworks doesn't store); and, for some customers, datasets and a subset of incomplete model weights. Fireworks says its inference, Training SDK, and Nexus products, which keep no data by default, were not affected.

This follows the first incident, found Oct 6, in which stolen internal credentials exposed environment variables (API keys and tokens) from evaluation jobs in some customer accounts. Fireworks says evidence points to a financially motivated group that resells model access through illicit gateways. It has notified law enforcement, brought in Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads for batch inference and dataset-based training, and moved lab-based training into an isolated environment. It hasn't said how many customers were hit or named the cloud provider.
**LLMjacking:** stealing API keys or cloud access to run AI models on someone else's bill, often reselling the access.
**Model weights:** the trained numbers that make up a model. 'Incomplete' here means partial or in-progress checkpoints, not full production models, per Fireworks.

Inference platforms hold three valuable things at once: customers' keys, customers' data, and customers' fine-tuned models. This is the second hit at Fireworks in three weeks and part of what Wiz called a 'Black October' of breaches across AI developer platforms. The weak point this time was a supplier's supplier, which no customer could have audited. If you use Fireworks, rotate any third-party credentials you stored there with their issuers (deleting the secret in Fireworks doesn't revoke it), and check for unfamiliar keys, users, jobs, or datasets.

stories.headline: Meta's Muse Ember matches Haiku's per-token price but is cheaper per task, by Meta's numbers
stories.summary: The fourth Muse model is a small, 1M-context workhorse for agent subtasks, built to take orders from the larger Muse Wonder.

p: On Monday, Nov 9, Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Ember, which Meta calls its lightest and most cost-efficient model. It is built for 'tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing,' the high-volume steps agents repeat. It takes text, images, audio, and video. Meta's pitch: 'Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.' It is available through the Meta Model API (`muse-ember-1.0`), Muse Code, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud. Meta hasn't said the weights are open.

Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 output, the same sticker price as Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna, with cheaper cached input ($0.004). Prompts over 200,000 tokens cost three times as much ($0.30/$1.50), which Meta's launch post leaves out but its pricing page lists. The real saving is in token use: on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Ember and Haiku 5.5 both score 36, but Ember used about 115 million output tokens to Haiku's 298 million, for roughly $0.14 versus $0.41 per task.

sections.note: Meta's figures at maximum reasoning effort, as reported by How2Shout and Fello AI. Meta ran several rows itself; the Artificial Analysis rows are the most independent.

p: The cheap-model tier is now a three-way tie on price, so the fight has moved to how many tokens a model needs to finish a job. That favors Ember on Meta's numbers, but Haiku still wins the one test of whether code is good enough to merge, which matters if you use these for coding subagents. Meta's Muse API is newer than OpenAI's or Anthropic's, with fewer integrations. Worth a test on your own workload before switching.

stories.headline: Meituan publishes LongCat-2.5's weights under the MIT license, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model built to run on Chinese chips
stories.summary: The open multimodal coding model made big gains over its predecessor, but still trails top US closed models on the hardest agent test.

p: On Nov 9, Meituan, the Chinese food-delivery giant, released the weights of LongCat-2.5 on Hugging Face under the MIT license, a week after introducing the model on Nov 2. It is a mixture-of-experts model with about 1.6 trillion total parameters and about 48 billion active per token (Hugging Face metadata says 1.8 trillion, a discrepancy Meituan hasn't explained). It handles screenshots, video, and code, and is aimed at long agent tasks such as visual coding. Meituan's hosted API costs $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.20 output at a limited-time rate, with a 1-million-token context. Its deployment guide targets Chinese accelerators, using 4-bit precision for expert weights.

sections.note: Meituan's figures as reported by VentureBeat. Its comparison models (Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) are older than today's frontier; Opus 5.5 scores 64.8 on the Terminal Bench 4.0 leaderboard under a different setup.

p: Another trillion-parameter Chinese open model under a fully permissive license, which keeps pressure on US closed-model pricing. The fair read: strong on older tests, a clear gap on the newest and hardest one, and compared against last-generation US models. At roughly 3 TB of weights at 16-bit precision, few teams can self-host it, but cloud hosts will. The detail to note is the hardware: Meituan is optimizing for domestic Chinese chips, part of China's push to get off Nvidia.

stories.headline: Google adds two new TPU systems, one built for confidential AI and one that packs two chips into a single package
stories.summary: TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max bring Google's eighth-generation chip family to four systems this year, aimed at regulated customers and long-context agents.

p: On Monday, Nov 9, Google announced two new members of its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) line in a blog post by Amin Vahdat, its chief technologist for AI infrastructure. They join TPU 8t (for training) and TPU 8i (for inference), which Google unveiled at Cloud Next in April. Google says this is the first time it has introduced four TPU systems in one year; historically it released a new chip roughly every two years.

**TPU 8tx** uses the same silicon as TPU 8t but is built for confidential workloads: it pairs with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts and encrypts data in hardware while it is being processed, which Google says carries a 'near-zero performance penalty.' It targets governments and regulated industries, can handle fine-tuning and small-scale training on private data, and Data Center Knowledge reports select customers can run it in their own data centers. **TPU 8i Max** puts two TPU 8i chips on one package, doubling compute, on-chip SRAM, and memory bandwidth versus a single 8i, and fitting twice the silicon in the same rack space. Google pitches it for 'massive context windows,' such as many agents working on one large codebase.

Google also released software: an open-source TPU agent suite that works with Claude Code, Cursor, and Antigravity; an XLA serving engine; TPU Sync, which it says cuts time to first token by more than 90%; and general availability of Cloud Pathways (the runtime behind Gemini) on Google Kubernetes Engine. Google gave no price or launch date for either chip. Bloomberg reports they are expected in 2027.

table: Up to 2x lower than TPU 8t (Google's network claim)
Up to 80% better inference price-performance (April claim)
Nearly 100, including Apple, Meta, and Oracle (Google, Gizmodo)
Up about 3% in premarket trading Monday
sections.note: Performance figures are Google's own and have not been independently tested. Availability timing is Bloomberg's reporting, not Google's.

p: **TPU:** Google's custom AI chip. Google doesn't sell TPUs; it rents them through Google Cloud.

**Confidential computing:** hardware that keeps data and model weights encrypted even while the chip is working on them, so the cloud operator can't read them. Until now it has mostly been a CPU feature; extending it to AI accelerators is newer.

**SRAM and HBM:** SRAM is small, very fast memory on the chip itself; HBM (high-bandwidth memory) is the larger stacked memory next to it. Long-context work is often limited by how fast data moves from memory, not by raw math.

These are variants, not a new generation. The 8tx is the old 8t silicon with secure CPU hosts and networking; the 8i Max is two existing chips glued together. That is a sensible way to answer customer requests quickly, and it shows where demand is moving: agents that hold huge amounts of context, and buyers (banks, health systems, governments) who won't send data to a cloud they can't verify. IDC's Dave McCarthy told Data Center Knowledge that Nvidia is still developing its own approach to confidential AI, which could give Google an opening.

Two caveats. Every number here is Google's, including the benchmark results it cites from InferenceX and AgentX. And with no price or date, and a reported 2027 arrival, this is a roadmap, not something customers can use this quarter. The timing, on the day Nvidia stock fell on the board's investigation of Jensen Huang, made it look like a challenge to Nvidia, but Google's TPU business was growing well before this week.
Pricing and availability for both systems, any independent benchmarks, and which regulated customers sign on for on-premises 8tx deployments.

stories.headline: Nvidia falls about 5% on its board's investigation of Jensen Huang while the rest of tech rebounds
stories.summary: The Nasdaq rose about 2.6% on Monday after last week's AI selloff, but Nvidia dropped as much as 8% as investors weighed what analysts call key-person risk.

p: Monday was Nvidia's first trading day since its board said on Sunday it would independently investigate reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, and since Huang told staff he had been unfaithful to his wife (covered in this morning's edition). Nvidia opened at $173.07, fell as much as 8% to an intraday low of $170.24, and was down about 5% around midday at roughly $176, versus Friday's close of $186.64. Reuters said a drop of that size would erase more than $250 billion in market value.

The broader market moved the other way. By about 2 p.m. ET the Nasdaq Composite was up about 2.6%, the S&P 500 about 2.4%, and chipmakers including AMD, Micron, and ASML rallied, partly reversing last week's selloff. In Asia, Nvidia supplier TSMC closed 4.7% higher. China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the spy allegations 'a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear.' President Trump told reporters on Sunday, 'I think he's an honorable guy,' and said he had not discussed it with Huang. In Seoul, Nvidia's AI Day went ahead without Huang, and his daughter Madison Huang canceled planned meetings there.

sections.note: Intraday figures from FinanceFeeds and Yahoo Finance's live blog; market value estimate from Reuters. Closing prices were not available when this edition was written.

p: **Key-person risk:** the risk that a company depends so heavily on one leader that losing or weakening them would hurt the business. Analysts are applying it to Huang, who has run Nvidia since founding it in 1993.

The market is treating this as an Nvidia problem, not an AI demand problem: suppliers and rival chipmakers rose. Most analysts quoted, including Dan Ives, who called it a 'black eye,' expect Huang to stay CEO. The real risks are slower-moving: findings from the board's outside counsel, congressional scrutiny over Megaspeed and China, and whether this complicates Nvidia's export license dealings with Washington.
One day's move says little on its own. The better test is Nvidia's Nov 17 earnings, where investors will look for any sign the controversy affects customers or guidance.
Nov 11 is the date the three House committee chairs asked Huang to confirm the Nov 18 briefing or offer another date. Earnings follow on Nov 17 at 5 p.m. ET.

stories.summary: Google's new K-12 controls let schools turn off Gemini but not the AI in Search, and a third senator is now pressing Sundar Pichai on it.
stats: Senators who have written Pichai on AI in schools

p: On Monday, Nov 9, Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) wrote to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai urging Google to give schools an AI-free version of Search and to drop the policy changes it announced for students, Bloomberg reported. Senators Josh Hawley and Richard Blumenthal sent an earlier letter on AI in classrooms on Oct 21.

The dispute started Nov 3, when Google's education chief Chris Phillips said Gemini and Search would be off for K-12 student accounts until administrators turned them on, and told The New York Times that schools rejecting AI would lose Search because 'Search and AI are deeply integrated.' After criticism from Sen. Bernie Sanders (who called it 'extortion'), former FTC chair Lina Khan, and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Google said within a day that Gemini and Search are 'separate controls,' so schools can enable Search without Gemini. But Search itself still comes with AI Overviews, which is what Markey wants removable. Google has not publicly responded to his letter.

**AI Overviews:** the AI-written summaries Google shows above regular search results. A university study cited this week found about 11% of their factual claims weren't supported by the sources they cite.

Google's partial reversal fixed the headline problem (losing Search) but not the underlying one: schools on Chromebooks and Google accounts can't easily switch search engines, so whatever Google bundles into Search reaches students by default. That is why critics frame it as a market-power issue, not just an education one, with Google already found to have violated antitrust law in search.

A letter has no legal force, but it adds to pressure from both parties, and Democrats take the House in January with plans for AI hearings. The cheapest fix for Google is a school setting that hides AI Overviews; watch whether it offers one before this becomes a hearing topic.

stories.headline: A Russian network used AI-cloned voices to exploit France's riots, an EU report says, but its reach was small next to domestic accounts
stories.summary: Operation Overload's top posts drew 2.8 million views, while the top MAGA-linked posts on the same unrest drew more than 49 million, according to documents seen by Reuters.

p: Reuters reported on Monday, Nov 9, on a restricted internal assessment by disinformation experts in the EU's diplomatic service, covering Oct 7 to 21, plus a separate French foreign ministry assessment. Both describe how 'Operation Overload,' a covert Russian network active since September 2023, exploited October's riots in France, which began over living costs and public services. It posted videos made to look like reports from Western news outlets, used AI to clone the voices of real experts, forged newspaper headlines, and pushed false claims that migrants had raped protesters or that terrorist attacks were imminent.

The EU found no evidence that Moscow started or escalated the protests, calling it 'opportunistic exploitation of unrest.' The French report says accounts linked to Israel and to the US MAGA movement also pushed 'hostile narratives' tying the riots to radical Islam and migration. Reuters could not independently verify either report, and Russia's foreign ministry did not respond.

sections.note: Figures from the EU and French assessments as reported by Reuters (via TimesLIVE).

p: **Voice cloning:** using an AI model to generate speech in a specific person's voice from a short sample. Here it put fake words in the mouths of real experts.

AI made this operation cheaper and more convincing (fake newscasts with familiar voices), but it did not make it the biggest voice in the room. The numbers suggest the larger amplification came from real, high-follower accounts. That matches what researchers have found before: AI lowers the cost of producing fakes, but distribution still depends on people and platforms.

For anyone building voice or video tools, this is the misuse case regulators cite most. The EU AI Act includes rules on labeling AI-generated deepfakes, and reports like this will feed arguments for enforcing them ahead of France's 2027 elections.

stories.headline: Nous Research retrains Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to stop repeating Chinese state positions, and says it cost almost no capability
stories.summary: Arete-27B is an open-weight fine-tune that Nous says cut propaganda-tagged answers from 22% to 0.9% on its own test, graded by one AI judge.

p: Late last week (Nov 6 to 7), Nous Research released Arete-27B on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. It is Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B with extra supervised fine-tuning that Nous says was meant to 'reinforce western values' on topics where Chinese-trained models tend to give the state's account, such as freedom of expression, state ideology, and democracy. Nous generated 20,000 training prompts across seven categories and used answers from Thinking Machines' open model Inkling as the teacher. Training used about 52.8 million tokens over 2 epochs, with no reinforcement learning or architecture changes.
Nous tested it on its own 803-prompt evaluation drawn from English-language statutes, news, and research reports. Grok 4.7 graded the answers without knowing which model wrote them.

sections.note: All numbers are Nous Research's own; no independent replication has been published.

p: **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT):** further training a model on example prompts and the answers you want, so it learns to imitate them.
**LLM judge:** using one AI model to grade another's answers. It's cheap and scalable but can share blind spots with the models it grades.

The interesting finding is how shallow the behavior appears to be: a small amount of fine-tuning shifted it a lot without hurting coding or agent scores. That matters for companies that want strong, cheap Chinese open-weight models but worry about their political defaults.

Treat the numbers carefully. Nous wrote the categories, the prompts, and the rubric, then trained on similar material, so some of the gain may be teaching to its own test. One AI judge did most of the grading and only 25 prompts were checked by hand. And 'western values' is a stated viewpoint, not neutrality: this swaps one set of defaults for another, which is fine if you know that's what you're getting.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang admits an affair in a memo to staff, and Nvidia's board opens an independent investigation
stories.summary: The board says it has no reason to think secrets were compromised, but Nvidia shares fell before Monday's open as the spy story moved from news reports to a formal company probe.

p: On Sunday, Nov 8, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sent employees a memo, later released publicly, in which he wrote: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children." and "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Reuters reported he did not give further details.

The same day Nvidia's board said it is "initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting" that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board said it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised and that its inquiry will "examine all available information." It did not name who will run the probe.

The backdrop: the New York Times reported last month that US intelligence believes Alice Huang (no relation), a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company under investigation over alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips into China, was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, and that surveillance of her revealed a close relationship with Huang. On Sunday the Times added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo warning senior officials about the relationship before President Trump's May trip to China. China's Foreign Ministry called the spy claims "purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear." Trump said he had not spoken with Huang, called him a fine person, and said he likely has an explanation.

table: Down more than 6%, about $270 billion off Friday's value (Reuters, LSEG data)
About 13% since the first reports on the Alice Huang relationship (Axios)
Closed-door, Nov 18, from three committee chairs
sections.note: Market figures from Axios and Reuters on Monday morning; premarket and overseas trading are thin and the regular session can differ.

p: **Independent board investigation:** a review run by directors who are not company executives, usually with outside lawyers, so the CEO is not investigating himself. It reports to the board, which decides whether to publish findings.
**Premarket trading:** US stock trades before the 9:30 a.m. ET open. Volume is low, so moves are a signal of sentiment, not a settled price.

Two separate questions are now tangled together. The affair is a personal and governance matter. The intelligence question is whether a suspected foreign agent got access to the CEO of the company at the center of US chip export policy. Huang's memo addresses the first and is silent on the second; the board's probe is aimed at the second. Note what the board did not say: that nothing happened, only that it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised.

For the AI industry the practical risk is policy, not product. Nvidia's case for selling H200-class chips into China leaned on Huang's personal standing in Washington. If Congress treats this as a security problem, expect tighter scrutiny of export licenses and of Nvidia's partners in Southeast Asia. Analysts' talk of succession is speculation for now: Huang has not stepped back and the board said nothing about his role. Asian chipmakers rising on the same day suggests investors see this as an Nvidia-specific problem rather than a hit to AI demand.

How the stock trades in the regular session, whether the board names outside counsel, whether Huang attends the requested Nov 18 House briefing, and Nvidia's quarterly results later this month, where analysts will ask about all of it.

stories.headline: Anthropic tells customers and Korea's privacy regulator what Cathedral's agents reached in its business systems
stories.summary: About 100 Korean corporate Claude accounts were in the exposed data, which Anthropic says covered names, emails, and plan details but not prompts, outputs, or payments.
stats: Time Cathedral says its agents needed

p: In late October, the Washington Post reported that Cathedral, a months-old security startup founded by four former DOGE staffers, told Anthropic its AI agents had found paths into Anthropic's internal business systems in under 12 hours. The way in was third-party sales, administrative, and HR software, not Claude itself. Anthropic said then that its monitoring flagged some of the activity, it cut off access the same day, and Claude conversations, source code, and model weights were not reached.

The new part is the notification. Anthropic began emailing affected customers around Nov 7; security researcher Jamieson O'Reilly posted his on X, which said Anthropic could not confirm whose information was viewed and that recipients face no heightened risk. On Nov 9, Yonhap and the Seoul Economic Daily reported that Anthropic told South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) on Oct 31 that account details for about 100 Korean corporate customers may have been exposed. An Anthropic staff member posted on X on Nov 8 that the data included account names, email addresses, and subscription plans, but not prompts, outputs, or payment data. The PIPC says it is doing a preliminary review and has not opened a formal investigation.

table: Account and organization IDs, names, business emails, plan tiers; some reports add usage and spend figures
Prompts, model outputs, payment data, source code, model weights
Under 12 hours (its draft report, per the Post)
$160 million at a $1.4 billion valuation, July 2026
sections.note: Figures from the Seoul Economic Daily, TechFlow (citing Yonhap), Runtime Wire, and Decrypt's summary of the Washington Post report.

p: **Third-party software risk:** a company's own systems can be locked down while a vendor's tool it uses (a CRM, an HR app) has a flaw that opens a door. Attackers often go through those side doors.
**PIPC:** South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission, which can investigate and fine companies that mishandle personal data of people in Korea, including foreign companies.

This is not a breach of Claude, but it is the kind of exposure that matters to enterprise buyers: who your company is, who your admins are, and what you pay. That is useful material for targeted phishing, which is why notices that say 'no heightened risk' deserve some skepticism. It also shows how quickly AI-driven penetration testing now finds weak points in ordinary business software, a pattern also seen in OpenAI's Hacktron episode, reported this weekend.

The dispute between the two companies remains. Anthropic said Cathedral overstated the national security angle and did not disclose all of its testing; Cathedral says it kept data access to a minimum. Neither side has published the full report. Timing matters too: Anthropic is trying to go public this month, and customer data notices land in risk-factor territory.
Whether the PIPC opens a formal probe, whether regulators elsewhere receive similar notices, and whether Anthropic's next IPO filing amendment mentions the incident.

stories.headline: Staff at the US government's AI testing center are informally reporting to the White House, AP reports
stories.summary: As Congress returns, the $10 million-a-year center has no permanent director and stopped publishing safety reports, and Trump told 60 Minutes that AI risk 'can be managed.'
stats: Its budget vs. the UK counterpart

p: The Associated Press reported on Sunday, Nov 8, that officials at CAISSI, the Commerce Department division that tests frontier AI models, were recently asked to report informally to a White House office, according to two former officials. CAISSI (now the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, until recently the Center for AI Standards and Innovation) has a budget of about $10 million a year, roughly one-eighth of the UK's equivalent. Its director was hired and fired within days in April, his replacement resigned after a few months, and it has had no permanent leader since. In August, Congress asked why it had stopped publishing reports on how AI systems performed in its tests.

The White House did not answer specific questions, pointing instead to the 'Super Intelligence Force' Trump created under National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. Separately, in a 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat that aired Sunday night, Trump said the risk of AI catastrophe "is not nearly as real" as portrayed and "can be managed," and that he doesn't "mind guardrails" but doesn't want the US in "a deep second position" to China.

**CAISSI:** the federal unit that runs voluntary pre-release tests of frontier models from labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. It was set up under Biden as the AI Safety Institute and has been renamed twice.
**Pre-deployment testing:** checking a model for dangerous capabilities (cyberattacks, bioweapons help, autonomy) before the public gets it. Labs grant access voluntarily and can limit it.

The government's main technical check on frontier models is small, leaderless, and now closer to political control, just as labs ship models with stronger cyber skills. Supporters say White House ties could raise its profile and funding; critics quoted by AP worry results could be muted or shaped. Either way, without published reports outsiders can't tell what testing is happening.

It also frames this week in Congress. OpenAI plans to push lawmakers for mandatory limits on the most powerful systems, and a newly Democratic House majority arrives in January. Trump's message is consistent: some guardrails are fine, falling behind China is not. Any bill that slows US labs without addressing China will face the White House.
Whether lawmakers in the lame-duck session move on CAISSI's funding or independence, and the administration's promised inventory of federal rules that apply to AI labs.

stories.headline: Nvidia, SK Telecom, and Rebellions agree to put Korean AI chips in Nvidia racks, linked by NVLink Fusion
stories.summary: The memorandum targets commercial data center deployment of Rebellions' R200 inference chip alongside Nvidia GPUs in 2028.

p: At Nvidia AI Day Seoul on Monday, Nov 9, Nvidia signed a memorandum of understanding with SK Telecom and Rebellions, a Korean AI chip startup, to build a combined GPU and NPU system. Several of Rebellions' next-generation R200 chips would be connected with NVLink Fusion, Nvidia's program that lets other companies' chips plug into its high-speed link, and housed in racks built to Nvidia's MGX server design. SK Telecom will validate the system on its infrastructure, with commercial deployment targeted for 2028.

Rebellions merged with Sapeon Korea, SK Telecom's former AI chip unit, in December 2024. Its CEO Park Sung-hyun said the partnership aims at "cost-competitive AI infrastructure." Reuters noted Madison Huang, Jensen Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled her planned Seoul visit; the event went ahead.

table: 4 stacks of HBM3E, 144GB, 4.8 TB/s memory bandwidth
Memorandum of understanding, not a purchase order
sections.note: Details from the Seoul Economic Daily.

p: **NPU (neural processing unit):** a chip built just for AI math, often tuned for inference (running models) rather than training. Simpler than a GPU, and often cheaper per answer.
**NVLink Fusion:** Nvidia opening its fast chip-to-chip connection to outside designs, so a customer can mix its own chips with Nvidia GPUs in one rack.
**MoU:** a statement of intent. It is not binding and doesn't commit anyone to buy.

Nvidia's strategy is visible here: if customers want cheaper inference chips, it would rather they run inside Nvidia racks, on Nvidia networking, than replace Nvidia altogether. For Korea, which wants homegrown 'sovereign AI' capacity, it gives a local chip a path into real data centers. But 2028 is a long way off, the R200's specs are unknown, and an MoU is the softest form of deal. Treat it as direction, not demand.

stories.headline: DeepSeek says its open-source agent framework, Harness, reached 1.54 million daily users
stories.summary: Daily users roughly tripled in a month, and DeepSeek says they burn about 92 trillion tokens a day, a sign of how much compute agents eat.
stats: Daily active users, week to Nov 4

p: DeepSeek disclosed usage numbers for Harness, its open-source agent framework, for the first time. It said Harness had 1.54 million daily active users on DeepSeek's official API in the week ended Nov 4, up from 429,000 in the week ended Oct 7 and 271,000 the week ended Sept 30. Users consume about 92 trillion tokens a day, and about 35,000 third-party plug-ins have been made, with roughly 60% of users creating or installing at least one. Bloomberg reported the figures on Nov 8; Yicai first reported them Nov 6.
DeepSeek describes Harness as the 'operating system' a model needs to act as an agent. On Oct 31 its team wrote about 'super-agents' that persist across sessions and run several tasks at once.

sections.note: Company-reported figures via Yicai and Bloomberg. Not independently audited.

p: **Agent harness:** the software around a model that lets it act: running tools, reading files, keeping memory, retrying, and planning steps. Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex are harnesses too.
**Daily active users (DAU):** distinct users in a day. Here it counts API usage, so many 'users' may be developers or automated setups, not people chatting.

The token figure is the real story. About 60 million tokens per user per day is far beyond what chat uses; it means agents running long loops, mostly unattended. That is the demand behind the data center build-out, and DeepSeek's low prices make long-running agents affordable. These are self-reported numbers from a company that doesn't publish audited figures, so take the growth curve as a direction. Still, it shows Chinese open-source agent tools gaining users quickly, not just Chinese models.

stories.headline: Anthropic agrees to pay $3.4 billion for 1.7 gigawatts of gas generators to power its data centers, FT reports
stories.summary: Anthropic took over a Texas supplier's stalled Caterpillar order, the largest known single purchase of power equipment by an AI company, though where the machines will run is not known.

p: The Financial Times reported on Sunday, Nov 8, that Anthropic agreed in late September to pay about $3.4 billion for 1.7 gigawatts of large gas-fired generators to power its data centers. The FT, citing one person with knowledge of the deal, called it the biggest known single purchase of power equipment by an AI company.

The counterparty is OnePWR Solutions, a power supplier in San Antonio, Texas. OnePWR had ordered the generators from Caterpillar about two years ago but needed money to complete the purchase. Anthropic first planned to buy electricity from OnePWR; instead it took over the Caterpillar orders, plus the engineering and construction work to install the machines. Anthropic did not buy OnePWR and no OnePWR staff moved over. Both companies declined to comment to the FT, and Reuters said it could not immediately verify the report.
The FT says it is not known where the generators will be used. The report does not give a delivery schedule, emissions figures, or permit filings.

table: About $2 billion per GW (Latent's arithmetic), including installation
Caterpillar (originally ordered by OnePWR about two years ago)
$895 billion, nearly all for compute and infrastructure (IPO filing, Nov 2)
sections.note: Deal figures from the Financial Times, as relayed by CNBC/Reuters and The Next Web. Commitments figure from Anthropic's amended IPO filing, covered in the Nov 3 Morning edition.

p: **Gigawatt (GW):** a billion watts. 1.7 GW running flat out is roughly the output of one and a half large nuclear reactors, and enough for several of today's biggest AI data center campuses.

**On-site (behind-the-meter) generation:** power produced at or next to the data center instead of drawn from the utility grid. It skips years-long waits to connect to the grid, but the owner takes on fuel, maintenance, and air-permit work.

**Reciprocating gas generators:** big engines (here, Caterpillar's) that burn natural gas to spin a generator. They start quickly and come in modular units, which is why AI builders are buying them alongside turbines and fuel cells.

The constraint on AI is now power as much as chips. Grid connections for large loads can take years, so labs are buying the generating equipment itself, and buying someone else's place in the order queue for it. Taking over an order placed two years ago is the point of the deal: Caterpillar and turbine makers have long backlogs, and a slot already in line is worth paying for.

It also shows Anthropic moving from renting compute toward owning pieces of the stack, weeks before a planned IPO. That cuts both ways for investors: more control over timelines, but more capital tied up and more exposure to a political fight. Gas-powered AI sites are drawing local opposition (xAI faces a lawsuit over turbines at its Memphis site), and the incoming Democratic Congress has named data center energy costs a priority. Treat the details as reported, not confirmed: the source is one person, and neither company has commented.
Whether the generators show up in an IPO filing update or a permit application, which would reveal the sites. Anthropic's roadshow timing is still unsettled.

stories.headline: Apple CEO John Ternus is pushing software chief Craig Federighi to move faster on AI agents, Bloomberg reports
stories.summary: Fixing Siri is 'no longer enough,' Ternus reportedly told Federighi, as Apple explores a Siri that can carry out multistep tasks on its own.

p: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in his Power On newsletter on Sunday that John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook as Apple CEO in September, held a closed-door meeting with software chief Craig Federighi in recent weeks and pressed him for a more ambitious AI roadmap. Ternus reportedly sees too little urgency compared with rivals and told Federighi that improving Siri is "no longer enough." Federighi is described by Gurman's sources as cautious about AI, citing privacy, security, and job concerns.

The rebuilt Siri that shipped in iOS 27 delivered much of what Apple promised in 2024 (personal context, on-screen awareness, actions inside apps), but it mostly responds to one command at a time. Apple is reportedly exploring a Siri that can pursue a goal through several steps without a new instruction each time, similar to the computer-use agents from OpenAI and Anthropic. Apple has not announced such a feature.

Gurman also reports that Apple is changing the development cycle for iOS 28 and its other major OS releases to give engineers more time to code and explore before features are merged, and that Siri engineering head Mike Rockwell is considering stepping back or leaving next year. Apple has not commented.

sections.note: From Apple's fiscal 2026 10-K filed Nov 3, as calculated by FourWeekMBA. Apple says the R&D rise was mainly higher infrastructure costs and headcount; it does not break out AI.

p: **Agentic AI:** an assistant that takes a goal ("rebook my flight and tell the hotel") and works through the steps itself, using apps and tools, instead of answering one request at a time.

**Computer use:** an agent that operates software the way a person does, reading the screen and clicking or typing. On a phone, Apple's version would more likely work through App Intents, the hooks apps expose so Siri can act inside them.

This is reporting from anonymous sources, but it fits the public record: Ternus called agentic AI "promising" on Apple's last earnings call, and Apple's own annual report this week warned that AI agents could act in unintended ways it cannot easily reverse. The tension is real. Apple's selling point is privacy and reliability, and agents that act on your behalf are where those are hardest to guarantee.

For developers, the practical signal is that Apple's agent push, if it comes, will run through apps that expose actions to Siri. Apps that already support App Intents would be first in line. Don't expect anything concrete before Apple's developer conference, usually held in June, and the iOS 28 schedule change suggests Apple is buying time rather than rushing.

stories.headline: OpenAI hires Hacktron, the firm that broke into its internal code with Claude's help, to probe its systems
stories.summary: Hacktron, paid a $6,500 bounty for a July attack chain that reached OpenAI's private repos, will test how OpenAI's services connect to outside platforms and gets OpenAI's restricted cyber models.
stats: OpenAI's time to fix SSO flaw

p: OpenAI announced a formal partnership with security firm Hacktron, which builds AI agents for code review and penetration testing. Engineers from both companies will pick test targets together, focusing on weaknesses "that arise when AI agents connect services in new ways": the links between ChatGPT and Codex and third-party apps, identity systems, and infrastructure. Hacktron also gets expanded access to OpenAI's purpose-built cyber models through its Daybreak Red program.

The backstory: on July 25, Hacktron reported to OpenAI's bug bounty an attack chain that started with a crafted image uploaded to OpenAI's Discourse community forum (exploiting a known flaw in the libheif image library), used an OpenAI single sign-on flaw to take over employees' ChatGPT and Codex accounts, and reached private internal repositories through a connected GitHub integration. The researchers proved access with a harmless pull request and stopped. OpenAI fixed its side about 14 hours after the report; Discourse patched two days after notice. OpenAI paid $6,500 on Sept 1. Hacktron's September writeup said it did most of the work with Anthropic's Opus models in under 72 hours and about $3,000 of tokens, with skilled humans steering.
**Single sign-on (SSO):** one login that unlocks many apps. A flaw there lets an attacker hop from a minor system (a help forum) to important ones.

**Daybreak Red:** OpenAI's restricted tier of cybersecurity models, including GPT-6 Cyber, for vetted organizations doing vulnerability research and exploit testing. Access requires identity checks and legal attestations.

Bringing in the people who embarrassed you is standard practice and a good sign. The more telling part is the focus. The weakest point in Hacktron's chain was not a model but the plumbing around it: a forum, a login system, and an agent connected to GitHub with broad permissions. That is the same pattern as this week's Claude Code secrets leak and the WorkOS incident. Anyone wiring agents into company systems should assume the integrations, not the model, are where attackers will go.

stories.headline: Claude Enterprise adds a security posture page and hooks that let company security tools check prompts and tool calls
stories.summary: Inference hooks are generally available; the Security Center, a company-wide admin console, and running endpoint security sensors inside Cowork are in beta.

p: Anthropic posted a set of Claude Enterprise admin updates on Nov 5. The headline feature for builders is **inference hooks**, now generally available: prompt hooks send prompts from supported Claude products to a company's security tool for checking, and pre-tool-call hooks check an agent's tool calls before they run, so existing data loss prevention policies can apply through supported security vendors.

In beta: a **Security Center** page that compares an organization's Claude settings with Anthropic's recommended configuration, shows each control's current and recommended value, and exports a report for auditors (Anthropic says it is guidance, not a compliance certification); a company-wide admin console at admin.claude.com for SSO, directory sync, and groups across multiple organizations; signing members out through the Admin API; self-serve IP allowlisting; and running a company's EDR sensor inside the Cowork virtual machine on macOS and Windows, in detection mode.
**DLP (data loss prevention):** software that spots and blocks sensitive data, such as customer records or passwords, leaving the company.

**EDR (endpoint detection and response):** security software on each computer that watches for malicious behavior. Running it inside Cowork's sandbox means the agent's actions are visible to the same tools that watch employees' laptops.

Pre-tool-call hooks are the meaningful piece: they put a company-controlled checkpoint between what an agent decides to do and what it actually does. That is the control the week's incidents argue for. Note what is missing: the hooks depend on supported vendors (Anthropic points to its Help Center for the list), the Security Center only checks Claude's own settings, and the posture page would not have caught the Claude Code permission-file leak, which lives in developers' repos.

stories.headline: Claude Code's 'don't ask again' file has leaked more than 1,300 passwords and keys into public GitHub repos, Apiiro finds
stories.summary: Approving a command once can save it, password and all, in a project file that often gets committed, and Microsoft says attackers' agents are already hunting GitHub for exactly these secrets.
stats: GitHub secret to Key Vault theft (Microsoft)

p: Security firm Apiiro published research, reported by The Hacker News on Saturday, showing how a Claude Code convenience feature leaks credentials. When Claude Code asks permission to run a shell command and you pick "Yes, and don't ask again," it writes an allow rule into `.claude/settings.local.json` inside the project. If the rule is a pattern like `npm test *`, that's harmless. If it is the exact command you approved, and that command had a password or token typed into it (for example after `PGPASSWORD=`, `sshpass -p`, or `mysql -p`), the secret is saved in plain text.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git by adding it to the user's global git excludes, but that only protects one machine and never touches the project's own `.gitignore`. Apiiro found 104,185 copies of the file in public repos; 1,122 of them contain at least one secret, 1,379 distinct secrets in total. In 539 of 1,105 repos it traced, the commit that changed the file listed Claude as co-author, which suggests the agent itself often commits it. Counting older git history, the shared `.claude/settings.json`, and saved agent chat logs, the total rises to 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories. Apiiro says it reproduced the behavior with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, and that of 16 coding agents it reviewed, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default.

Apiiro says the behavior was reported to Anthropic on GitHub in August 2025 (issue #5544), that an automated bot closed it as "not planned" after 60 days of inactivity, and that four related reports met the same fate. No Anthropic response or fix was reported as of Saturday. Separately, Microsoft Threat Intelligence wrote on Nov 5 that attackers using the ARTEX agent framework have been searching GitHub for secrets since August, and in one case went from finding a client secret to pulling data out of Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

table: Copies of settings.local.json in public repos
Copies holding at least one secret
Files neither gitleaks nor TruffleHog flagged
Total incl. history, shared settings, chat logs
sections.note: Apiiro's figures as reported by The Hacker News. Apiiro did not test whether the secrets still work; one notified company confirmed its key was live.

p: **Allowlist rule:** a saved permission telling an agent it may run a command without asking. A pattern rule (`Bash(npm run:*)`) covers a family of commands; an exact rule stores the literal command text.
**Global git excludes:** a per-user ignore list on one computer. Unlike a repo's `.gitignore`, it does nothing for teammates, CI, or files already committed.

**Secret scanning:** tools like gitleaks and TruffleHog that look for keys in code. They are good at recognizable token formats and bad at a bare password typed after a flag, which is why they missed 215 of these files.
**Service principal:** a non-human identity an app uses to log in to a cloud. A leaked client secret for one lets an attacker act as that app.

This is a design default, not a clever exploit: the agent writes secrets into a file inside the repo and sometimes commits that file itself. The fix for users is cheap, but the scale shows that the safety of agent tools depends on boring defaults like where approvals are stored. It also undercuts the common assumption that the risk of coding agents is what they do on their own; here the leak comes from a human clicking a helpful button.

Pair it with Microsoft's report and the window between "secret pushed to GitHub" and "secret used" is now minutes, because attackers run agents too. Deleting the file later does not help, since it stays in git history and forks. Any password or key that ever sat in one of these files should be treated as stolen and rotated.
Caveat: Apiiro sells application security tools, and these are its counts. They are specific and checkable, though, and the mechanism is easy to reproduce.

list: Search your repos, including history, for `.claude/settings.local.json` and `.claude/settings.json`.
Rotate every credential those files ever contained before cleaning up.
Run `git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json` and add it to the repo's `.gitignore`.
Approve command patterns, not one-off commands with secrets in them, and pass secrets through environment variables from a secrets manager.
Treat agent folders (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.gemini/`) like `.env` files in pre-commit and CI scanning.

p: Whether Anthropic changes the default (for example, storing approvals outside the project, or writing patterns instead of literal commands) and reopens the closed GitHub issues.

stories.headline: US cleared Chinese firms with empty offices and blacklist ties to build Nvidia H200 servers, NYT reports
stories.summary: Two of roughly two dozen approved licensees appear to have no real presence at their listed addresses, and others have owners linked to firms serving China's military.

p: The New York Times reported Saturday that the Commerce Department approved a Chinese company called New Matrix this year to assemble Nvidia H200 chips into AI servers, and that its listed office in an industrial park on Beijing's northwest edge is "a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be." Chinese corporate records link New Matrix's owners to Wise Road, a private equity fund the US put on its entity list in 2024. The company was set up 17 months ago and did not respond to the Times. Two analysts told the paper it may be a front for firms tied to that fund.

A second licensee, Maginfra, appeared deserted when the Times visited in September; analysts believe it is an offshoot of Inspur, which is on the entity list for work with China's military. The Times also said two more licensees, Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology and Shanghai Jiatang, have owners tied to firms that serve the military. According to people familiar with the approvals, about two dozen Chinese firms were cleared, including Baidu, BYD, and Tesla Shanghai, each for tens of thousands of chips, and none has yet hit its quota.

The Bureau of Industry and Security said it carefully reviews every application, imposed $324 million in export-violation penalties in 2025, and hired more than 90 enforcement officers this year. Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo said it "makes no sense for the Chinese military to depend on American technology."

table: Chinese firms reportedly approved for H200s
US cut on H200 sales to China
25% tariff, collected as chips route through the US
H200 shipments to China, quarter ending July
Under 1% of Nvidia data center revenue
sections.note: From the New York Times as summarized by FourWeekMBA. The full licensee list has not been published; the total comes from unnamed people familiar with the approvals.

p: **Entity list:** the Commerce Department's list of foreign companies that need a special license to receive US technology, usually over national security concerns.
**Front company:** a firm that exists on paper to let another, often restricted, company buy what it can't buy directly.
**H200:** an Nvidia data center GPU one generation behind its newest chips. Trump allowed its sale to China in December, with the US government taking a cut.

The H200 policy rests on the idea that licenses plus vetting keep chips away from blacklisted buyers. This report suggests the vetting is thin: an empty shell with owners tied to an entity-listed fund got approved. Nothing here is proven wrongdoing; the Times did not establish who controls New Matrix, no licenses have been revoked, and the licenses cover assembling servers, not final sales. But it lands the same week as the Megaspeed spy allegation and adds to pressure on both Commerce and Nvidia.

In practice, the China H200 business is still tiny for Nvidia (under 1% of data center revenue last reported quarter). The bigger risk is political: tighter rules or license reviews could follow, and this gives lawmakers a concrete example.
Calls for an audit of the licenses, and whether the topic comes up at the House chairs' requested Nov 18 briefing with Jensen Huang.

stories.headline: AI safety PACs mostly backed midterm winners; the industry-funded network's biggest bets lost
stories.summary: An FEC count finds 97.5% of the Anthropic-backed Public First network's general-election money went to races that ended its way, versus 52.6% for Leading the Future.
stats: Public First money on winning side
Leading the Future money on winning side
LTF network spend on one losing Senate race

p: With the midterm results mostly called, the two rival AI super PAC networks can be scored. **Public First**, backed by Anthropic, wants stronger AI rules and keeps states' power to pass them. **Leading the Future (LTF)**, backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Andreessen Horowitz, wants one national framework that would override state laws. Bloomberg reported Saturday that candidates favoring stricter AI oversight won key congressional races, and that Public First said it put more than $63 million into the midterms (the group's own figure).

A FourWeekMBA count of FEC independent-expenditure filings through Oct 30, matched to AP race calls, found Public First's network spent $10.54 million across 13 general-election races, mostly opposing candidates, and 12 of 13 went its way. LTF's network spent $9.31 million across 22 races, all supporting candidates, and 19 of 20 called races went its way, but its one big loss, South Carolina's Senate race, swallowed most of its money. TechCrunch reported LTF's Republican arm also spent over $500,000 each on House candidates Aaron Flint (Montana) and Laurie Buckhout (North Carolina), who both lost, while Guardrails Alliance, a group that attacks candidates for taking AI industry money, helped defeat California Rep. Jimmy Gomez.

table: Races that went Public First's way
LTF spend on Darline Graham (SC Senate, lost)
Public First's claimed total cycle spending
sections.note: FourWeekMBA's analysis of FEC 24/48-hour reports and AP calls as of Nov 7; spending after Oct 30 is excluded. Primary and race details from TechCrunch.

p: **Super PAC:** a political committee that can raise and spend unlimited money on ads for or against candidates, as long as it doesn't coordinate with campaigns.
**Independent expenditure:** the spending super PACs must report to the FEC within 24 or 48 hours close to an election. It shows where money went, not who gave it.
**Preemption:** a federal law overriding state laws on the same topic. It is the core fight between the two networks.

Don't read the win rate as proof that AI money decided races. Public First mostly spent against candidates in a strong Democratic year, and TechCrunch notes it is hard to separate AI spending from the broader wave. The dollar-weighted scores are also skewed by one race on each side. What the numbers do show is that the pro-regulation camp chose its general-election races well, and that LTF put its money mostly into primaries, where it says name recognition matters more.

For people building with AI, the practical stake is preemption. A Congress less friendly to a single light-touch federal rule makes it more likely that state laws, like California's and New York's, keep applying and keep multiplying.
Congress returns Monday, Nov 9, and OpenAI plans a lame-duck push for federal "speed limits" on the most powerful AI systems. Both networks say they will keep spending in 2028.

stories.headline: Eminem's publisher and Elvis Presley's rights holders sue Suno, one over copyright and one over voice imitation
stories.summary: Eight Mile Style says Suno copied 269 compositions and seeks damages that could top $40 million; the Presley suit leans on Tennessee's ELVIS Act.

p: Eight Mile Style, the Michigan publisher that controls much of Eminem's catalog, sued AI music generator Suno on Friday in federal court in the Northern District of California, CBS News reported. It claims direct copyright infringement over 269 compositions, circumvention of copy protections, and removal of copyright management information. Citing a 404 Media report, it alleges Suno scraped songs and lyrics from YouTube Music, Deezer, and Genius, and gives an example of a generated track that reproduces an Eminem lyric word for word. It asks for a willful infringement finding, destruction of unauthorized copies, and damages that could exceed $40 million. Eminem himself is not a plaintiff.

Separately, rights holders for Elvis Presley, including Authentic Brands Group and Raleigh Music Publishing, filed a 51-page complaint in federal court in California saying Suno lets users generate songs that imitate Presley's voice and musical identity, invoking Tennessee's 2024 ELVIS Act. Suno told CBS it prohibits "any unauthorized use of an artist's work," blocks prompts naming specific artists or songs, and screens uploads; it has argued in other cases that training is fair use.

**Copyright vs. right of publicity:** copyright protects a specific work (a song's lyrics and melody, a recording). The right of publicity protects a person's identity, such as their name, likeness, and voice. A model can avoid copying any song and still violate publicity rights by sounding like a specific singer.
**ELVIS Act:** a 2024 Tennessee law that explicitly adds a person's voice, including an AI simulation of it, to the state's publicity-rights protections.
**Copyright management information:** credits and metadata attached to a work. Stripping it can be a separate violation under the DMCA.

Suno already faces suits from labels and a class action from musicians over publicity rights; this adds a publisher with a verbatim-lyrics example, which is harder to defend as fair use than a general training claim. The two filings show the two legal routes rights holders now use against AI music: copying the works, and copying the artist. The second doesn't depend on how courts rule on training, which makes it the more durable threat to voice-cloning features.
Nothing is proven yet; these are complaints. The same Presley rights group separately sued Anthropic over 274 songs last month, so this is a coordinated campaign, not a one-off.
Suno's response and any motion to dismiss, and whether other publishers join. The EU and US courts are also still working out whether training itself is allowed.

stories.headline: Microsoft's AI Frontiers lab, which built AutoGen, is over, says its departing leader John Langford
stories.summary: The roughly 50-person research group was folded into Microsoft AI in September; Langford says its ideas couldn't get used there, and AutoGen no longer gets security fixes.

p: John Langford, a well-known machine learning researcher, wrote on his blog on Nov 6 that "AI Frontiers is over" and that he has left Microsoft. He co-founded the group inside Microsoft Research in 2023, after ChatGPT, and it grew to about 50 people. Its work focused on making agents work, including the AutoGen multi-agent framework and Fara, a computer-use agent. In early September the group was moved into Microsoft AI, the model-building division. Langford described a clash between scaling and research, said leadership's focus was on getting, making, and refining data, and that his group's innovations couldn't get used or seriously considered. "So I situated my folks as best I could and left," he wrote. There will be no internships with the group next year.

AutoGen was already winding down: since an Oct 16 README change, Microsoft says it is "not providing bug fixes, security fixes, new features, or support," and points users to Microsoft Agent Framework, which shipped 1.0 in April.
**AutoGen:** an open-source Python framework for building systems where several AI agents talk to each other to finish a task. It was one of the most popular early agent frameworks.
**Microsoft Agent Framework:** Microsoft's newer, supported agent SDK for .NET and Python that replaces AutoGen and Semantic Kernel.
**Scaling vs. research:** the tension between putting resources into bigger models and more data, which reliably improves results, and into new methods that may or may not pay off.

It fits a pattern: Google, Meta, and now Microsoft have moved independent AI research groups under product or model teams, and researchers who want to explore leave. For Microsoft, it signals Microsoft AI is concentrating on building its own frontier models, which matters as Microsoft reportedly winds down a server rental deal with Oracle.

For developers, the practical point is AutoGen: if you still run it, you are on unmaintained code with no security patches, and the GitHub repo isn't marked archived, so automated checks may miss that. Note that the `autogen` package on PyPI belongs to AG2, a separate community fork.

stories.headline: US intelligence believes an Nvidia cloud partner executive close to Jensen Huang worked for China's spy agency, NYT reports
stories.summary: The allegation centers on Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that buys Nvidia chips, and lands the same day Bloomberg reports Nvidia is tying partner status in Southeast Asia to chip location tracking.

p: The New York Times reported Friday that US intelligence officials told the Trump administration that Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, had become close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and was working for China's Ministry of State Security (MSS). According to the Times, cited by Bloomberg, the MSS wanted to learn more about US AI chips and possibly to persuade Nvidia to make its most advanced chips available to China. The Times reported US agencies conducted electronic surveillance of her for about a year and that President Trump was briefed in 2025. These are allegations from unnamed sources; the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not comment.

Megaspeed is part of Nvidia's cloud partner network: it buys Nvidia hardware and rents computing to AI developers. It has been under US and Singaporean investigation for more than a year over suspected diversion of chips to China, and has denied wrongdoing. Nvidia said after the report that its cloud partners "do not ask us to seek changes in US law or advocate for sales to China" and that "We neither have nor share classified information with customers." Jensen Huang has previously called the company's dealings with Megaspeed normal and said Nvidia checked that Megaspeed did not illegally send chips to China.

Separately on Friday, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia now requires Southeast Asian cloud providers that want official Nvidia Cloud Partner status to enroll in its fleet tracking software, which can report where individual accelerators are located. House lawmakers, led by the Select Committee on China, have asked Huang for a closed-door briefing on Megaspeed.

table: Restricted Nvidia GPUs traced through regional routes, 2022 to 2025
Servers allegedly diverted to China in the Super Micro case
Malaysian capacity a landlord took back from Megaspeed in April
Reported US surveillance of the executive
sections.note: C4ADS, prosecutor, and Malaysia figures as reported by Tom's Hardware, citing Bloomberg and earlier reporting. Surveillance detail from the New York Times as relayed by Bloomberg and The Week.

p: **Nvidia Cloud Partner (NCP):** an official Nvidia designation for companies that rent out Nvidia-powered computing. It comes with Nvidia's endorsement and preferred access to scarce chips.
**Chip diversion:** restricted chips sold to a legal buyer in one country, then moved or rented to a buyer the export rules are meant to block, often through a third country.
**Location verification:** software that estimates where a GPU is physically running, using telemetry and network delay measurements. Nvidia describes it as an opt-in tool customers install.

Nothing here is a charge or a finding of wrongdoing by Nvidia or Jensen Huang, and the central claim rests on unnamed intelligence sources. But it lands at a bad moment for Nvidia: Huang has been the loudest voice for loosening chip exports to China, a Democratic House takes over in January, and Bloomberg reported this week that Democrats plan more oversight of Nvidia's exports and financing deals.

The tracking requirement is the more concrete change. Southeast Asia has been the main transit route for restricted chips, and making location reporting a condition of partner status is Nvidia's strongest step yet to show it can police its own customers. It is still limited: it applies to partner status in one region, participation elsewhere is voluntary, and Nvidia has not said whether existing partners must enroll.
Whether Huang agrees to the briefing, whether Congress or Commerce writes location verification into export rules, and any action from the US or Singapore investigations into Megaspeed.

stories.headline: Anthropic's agent memory study: stronger models keep fewer notes and do better, and a background 'dreaming' pass fixes mistakes
stories.summary: An engineering post with experiments on databases, Pokemon Red, and a 420 million token codebase shows memory helps newer Claude models a lot, but rigid rules about what to save hurt.

p: Anthropic published "The components of agent memory" on November 6, written by Lance Martin. It defines agent memory as knowledge an agent gains from experience and keeps across sessions as readable files, not changes to the model's weights. It describes four layers: raw transcripts (a searchable log), notes the agent writes, larger structures such as wikis built from those notes, and a small amount of context injected into every session.

The post's main idea is **dreaming**: a background process that rereads an agent's logs while it is idle, corrects wrong notes, and builds better summaries, modeled on how sleep helps people consolidate memories. It builds on 'sleep-time compute' work from Letta and UC Berkeley. Dreaming is already offered in Claude Managed Agents, with cookbooks for it and for knowledge wikis.

In Pokemon Red, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files in 225 folders over about 10,000 steps and earned one badge; much of what it saved went stale. Fable 5 kept nine files in two folders, saved only things the screen did not show (plans, tested rules), and earned four badges. Opus 5.5 used a similarly lean approach and beat the game. In one test, a wrong note about a Pokemon Center made the agent loop; after a dreaming pass checked notes against transcripts, it reached Cerulean City at action 1,935. Without memory it never got there.

table: Codebase Q&A, dreamed wiki plus search
Legal merger questions, wiki vs search alone
'Record only failures' rule, lost memory gain (Opus 5)
sections.note: All figures from Anthropic's post. Database task is CL-Bench (mean reward). Codebase corpus is about 350,000 files (~420M tokens) from Stainless, graded on 25 questions; legal set is 24 Harvey LAB questions.

p: **Salience:** how important a piece of information will turn out to be. An agent has to guess this when it decides what to write down, before it knows what will matter.
**Sleep-time compute:** spending compute while an agent is idle to reorganize what it learned, so later sessions start from better notes.

**Injected context:** the small set of instructions and memory loaded into every session. Anthropic notes Claude Code reads only the first 200 lines or 25 KB of its MEMORY.md index, because long instruction files lower how well models follow them.

The useful finding for builders is that memory design should depend on the model. Newer models did best when simply told a memory folder exists; a fixed rule like 'record only failures' cost Opus 5 a large part of its gain. Older models needed explicit steering: Sonnet 5 reads memory before answering 9 times in 10, versus under half the time for Sonnet 4.6.

Keep the limits in mind. These are Anthropic's own tests on Anthropic models, several on small question sets (24 to 25 questions), and some results cut the other way: on one legal task the generated wiki ended up 1.77 times larger than the source documents and gave no clear gain on single-document questions. Dreaming also costs compute. The post itself says Anthropic still has much to learn, and that plain transcript search is a strong baseline that wikis only modestly beat.
Whether dreaming moves from Managed Agents into Claude Code and the Claude apps, and whether outside teams reproduce the gains on non-Anthropic models.

p: Bloomberg reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter, that Microsoft chose not to renew a 2023 agreement to rent Oracle cloud servers, which it used to run AI features in Bing, and has been switching that capacity off in recent months. The sources said the servers used older Nvidia chips that no longer fit Microsoft's needs. Bloomberg could not determine the deal's full size.

Microsoft declined to comment. Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains "strong," including for older chips. Separate talks for Microsoft to lease more Oracle capacity collapsed in June, according to Business Insider.

table: Oracle share move on the report
Microsoft commitments to rent capacity from others
More than $80B (CoreWeave, Nscale, Nebius and others)
sections.note: Figures from Bloomberg's report as summarized by The Next Web.

p: **Neocloud / rented capacity:** instead of building every data center itself, a big cloud company can rent GPU servers from another provider. It is faster, but the renter does not control which chips it gets or how long they stay useful.
**Depreciation risk:** AI chips lose value quickly as newer generations arrive. If customers stop wanting older chips, the owner may have to write down their value.

On its own this is one older contract. The pattern matters more: this week Microsoft passed on doubling a Texas deal with Nscale, weeks after leaving an Nscale site in the UK, and Bloomberg reports its leaders are frustrated with costs and delays at rental providers. Microsoft appears to be shedding capacity it no longer wants rather than stopping AI spending.

For Oracle the story is sharper, because its bet depends on long-lived demand for the servers it has bought with heavy borrowing. Its free cash flow is negative and its credit rating sits one notch above junk, per the same reporting. A big customer walking away from older-chip capacity is exactly the risk analysts have flagged.
Oracle's fiscal Q2 results on December 14, and whether other hyperscalers trim rented older-generation capacity.

stories.headline: Google's $17 billion Wyoming campus is on a site it bought from Crusoe
stories.summary: Crusoe, which had pitched the site to customers, sold it to Google after doing the permits and power planning; the price was not disclosed.

p: A day after Google announced a $17 billion data center in Wyoming, Crusoe said on November 6 that Google had acquired its southeast Wyoming site. Crusoe and Tallgrass Energy had started the campus together, and Crusoe says the sale completes its pre-development work: choosing the site, getting government approvals, and planning power. Terms were not disclosed, Reuters reported.

Bloomberg reported that Crusoe had pitched the site to other customers before Google took it over. Google will build with Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power, and Related Digital. The planned power mix combines fuel cells, grid power, and gas turbines, with long-term plans to capture carbon through Tallgrass's sequestration hub.

**Entitlement:** the permits, zoning, and approvals needed before construction. For data centers, securing land, power, and permits is often the slowest part, so developers can profit by doing that work and then selling the site.

This fills in Thursday's story: Google did not start from scratch in Wyoming; it bought a site already through the hardest early steps. It also shows how the AI build-out is shaking out. Developers like Crusoe take the permitting and power risk, and the companies with the cash and the demand (here, Google) end up owning the campuses. A site that was being shopped to customers is also a reminder that not every planned AI data center has a customer lined up.
